title: Perilous Times and the Sufficient Word
summary: Paul exposes hollow, self-loving religion in the last days and anchors Timothy in apostolic example and God-breathed Scripture.
historicalContext: Paul writes from a Roman prison with his execution in view (4:6), while Timothy labors in Ephesus amid a crisis the apostle had foreseen when he warned the Ephesian elders that ravenous wolves would arise from within (Acts 20:29–30). Teachers such as Hymenaeus and Philetus were unsettling households with speculation and a denial of the future resurrection (2:17–18), and many in Asia had turned from Paul (1:15). Believers met in homes, so a teacher who gained entry to a household could reach a congregation. Ephesus was notorious for magical arts (Acts 19:19), which gives sharp edge to Paul’s comparison with Pharaoh’s sorcerers. Timothy himself came from Lystra, where he had seen what preaching Christ cost Paul on the first missionary journey, and he had been taught Israel’s Scriptures from infancy by a Jewish mother and grandmother (1:5; Acts 16:1).
literaryContext: Chapter 2 closed with the hope that God might grant opponents repentance; chapter 3 sets beside that hope a sober reading of the age. The first movement (vv. 1–9) portrays people of the last days in a catalogue framed by misdirected loves, then applies it to teachers who infiltrate homes and resist the truth like the magicians who withstood Moses. The second movement turns on two emphatic addresses, “But thou” (vv. 10, 14), setting Timothy against that backdrop: he has followed Paul’s teaching and sufferings, and he must remain in what he learned from the holy Scriptures. A thread of “progress” runs through the letter—error spreads (2:16), yet it is checked (3:9), even as evildoers advance only toward the worse (3:13). The chapter’s praise of God-breathed Scripture supplies the content for the charge that follows, “Preach the word” (4:2).
themes: The moral danger of the last days
Misdirected love as the root of corruption
Religious form emptied of saving power
Counterfeit truth and its certain exposure
Faithful example and the cost of godliness
God-breathed Scripture that saves and equips

outline.title: Portrait of the Last Days
outline.summary: Paul warns of hard times marked by self-love, broken relationships, and religion that keeps its form while refusing its power.

outline.title: Counterfeit Teachers and Their Limit
outline.summary: False teachers prey on burdened households and resist the truth like Pharaoh’s magicians, but their folly will be exposed.

outline.title: An Apostle’s Life and the Path of Persecution
outline.summary: Timothy has followed Paul’s teaching, conduct, and sufferings, and learns that all who live godly in Christ will face persecution while deceivers worsen.

outline.title: Remaining in the God-Breathed Word
outline.summary: Timothy must continue in the Scriptures he has known from childhood, which make wise unto salvation and fully equip the man of God.

verses.bibleText: This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul has just expressed the hope that God may grant repentance to those who oppose the truth and free them from the devil’s snare (2:25–26). Now he places a sober counterweight beside that hope. “This know also” is a present imperative: Timothy must keep this understanding steadily before him. Gentleness toward opponents must never become naivety about the age in which the gospel is preached.

“In the last days” is not a period reserved for some remote future. Peter declared at Pentecost that the last days had arrived with the outpouring of the Spirit (Acts 2:17), and Hebrews says God has spoken “in these last days” by his Son (Hebrews 1:2). Paul himself shifts into the present tense in verse 6, showing that Timothy already faces the people he describes. Yet the expression also looks forward. Jesus taught that lawlessness would increase and love grow cold before the end (Matthew 24:12), and verse 13 of this chapter speaks of evil men growing worse. The whole era between Christ’s ascension and his return bears these marks, with mounting intensity as Satan, knowing his time is short, presses the conflict toward its climax (Revelation 12:12).

“Perilous times” renders a phrase meaning hard, harsh, or dangerous seasons. The danger Paul has in mind is chiefly moral. The next verse begins “For men shall be,” locating the peril in what people become. The deepest threat to the church is not the hostility of governments but the corruption of character, including character inside the congregation.

wordNotes.term: ἐν ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις (en eschatais hēmerais) — in the last days
wordNotes.explanation: Drawn from the prophets’ language for the time of God’s decisive action, the phrase in the New Testament designates the age opened by Christ’s coming and the gift of the Spirit. It is both present and intensifying: the apostles lived in it, and its features grow sharper as the Lord’s return draws near.

Kairoi refers to seasons or periods rather than a single moment, and chalepos means hard, troublesome, or dangerous. Its only other New Testament use describes two violent demoniacs whom travelers could not safely pass, suggesting times made savage by what people become.

verses.bibleText: For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The word “For” introduces the reason the times will be hard: people themselves will be marked by a long catalogue of vices. In the Greek the list runs without connecting words, item after item, so that the effect is cumulative. Not every person displays every trait, but together they form a portrait of humanity turned away from God. The list opens and closes with words about love. It begins with “lovers of their own selves” and “covetous,” literally lovers of money, and it ends in verse 4 with “lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God.” The frame is deliberate. Sin at its root is love aimed at the wrong object. When the self sits at the center, love for God and neighbor—the two great commandments—is displaced, and the remaining vices follow naturally. Love of money was already a defining trait of the false teachers in Ephesus, who treated godliness as a means of gain (1 Timothy 6:5–10).

“Boasters” are those who claim more than is true about themselves, and the “proud” look down on others from a self-made height; God sets himself against such people (James 4:6). “Blasphemers” here includes abusive speech aimed at other people as well as irreverence toward God. “Disobedient to parents” strikes at the fifth commandment, the first with a promise (Ephesians 6:2), and signals the breakdown of the home on which wider society rests. “Unthankful” recalls Paul’s account of humanity’s descent in Romans: they knew God but did not glorify him or give thanks (Romans 1:21). “Unholy” describes a life with nothing held sacred.

The resemblance to Romans 1:29–31 is striking, but there Paul describes pagan society; here, as verse 5 will reveal, these traits appear among people who keep a form of godliness. The list is therefore first a mirror. The self-love it exposes is the very thing the gospel crucifies, so that the believer can say, “I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me” (Galatians 2:20).

wordNotes.term: φίλαυτοι (philautoi) — lovers of their own selves
wordNotes.explanation: The compound joins “loving” to “self” and stands first in the list as the source of what follows. It describes a life organized around one’s own interests, the opposite of love that “seeketh not her own” and of the mind that looks to the things of others.

The negative prefix denies gratitude, the fitting response to grace received. Jesus noted that God remains kind to the unthankful, while Paul traces humanity’s decline to a refusal to give thanks to the Creator who gives all things.

verses.bibleText: Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Most of the words in this verse are formed with a negative prefix, each one naming the absence of something God ordinarily preserves even in fallen human life. They describe people stripped of the restraints and affections that make society bearable.

“Without natural affection” denies the instinctive love that binds parents and children. When even that tie fails, little else holds. “Trucebreakers” is better rendered irreconcilable: people who will not make peace or accept terms, whose hostility admits no settlement. The contrast with the gospel is plain, for God has given his people the ministry of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18–20).

“False accusers” translates diaboloi, the plural of the word used for the devil himself. Paul has just spoken of those taken captive by the devil at his will (2:26); here the captives come to resemble their captor. The accuser of the brethren reproduces his character in people who slander and tear down others. In the great conflict between Christ and Satan, character always reveals which master a person serves (John 8:44).

“Incontinent” means without self-control, ruled by appetite and impulse instead of principle. Scripture treats mastery of the body’s desires as a fruit of the Spirit and a requirement for leaders (Galatians 5:23; Titus 1:8), because a life governed by craving cannot remain open to God. “Fierce” means untamed or savage, humanity reduced to the level of a beast. “Despisers of those that are good” describes people who have no love for goodness and resent those who practice it. The opposite quality, “a lover of good men,” appears among the marks required of an elder (Titus 1:8).

Taken together, these terms show how far sin reaches beyond the private self. It unravels families, hardens conflicts, poisons speech, and turns people against goodness itself.

wordNotes.explanation: The word means slanderers, those who spread damaging accusations. It is the term that, in the singular with the article, names the devil. The Pastorals warn church members against this sin and expect older women to be free of it.

Formed from a word for power or mastery with a negative prefix, it describes people lacking control over their own desires. Its opposite, self-mastery, is part of the Spirit’s fruit and part of the disciplined life Paul likens to an athlete’s training.

verses.bibleText: Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Traitors” are betrayers, people who hand others over for their own advantage. Luke uses the word of Judas, and Stephen uses it of those who betrayed the Righteous One (Luke 6:16; Acts 7:52). Jesus warned that in the time before the end many would betray one another (Matthew 24:10). Where self-love rules, loyalty becomes negotiable.

“Heady” describes people who rush headlong, reckless and impulsive. The same word appears in the counsel of the town clerk of Ephesus, who urged the crowd to do nothing rashly (Acts 19:36), a phrase Timothy’s own city had heard. “Highminded” means puffed up or clouded with conceit, a danger Paul has already named for new converts in leadership and for teachers who love controversy (1 Timothy 3:6; 6:4).

The catalogue then reaches its summary: “lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God.” The comparison does not mean that these people love God a little and pleasure somewhat more. The construction carries the force of “instead of.” Pleasure has taken God’s place. Scripture does not treat enjoyment as evil; God “giveth us richly all things to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17). The disorder lies in making pleasure the governing love, the thing for which everything else is sacrificed. Jesus described seed choked by the pleasures of this life (Luke 8:14), and Paul admitted that before grace appeared he too had served “divers lusts and pleasures” (Titus 3:3).

God’s own counsel offers a way to retrain the heart. Through Isaiah he called his people to turn from doing their own pleasure on his holy day and to call the Sabbath a delight, promising that they would then delight themselves in the Lord (Isaiah 58:13–14). Weekly worship, rest, and fellowship with God loosen pleasure’s grip by giving the heart a higher joy. The cure for disordered love is not the absence of delight but delight placed in God.

wordNotes.term: φιλήδονοι μᾶλλον ἢ φιλόθεοι (philēdonoi mallon ē philotheoi) — lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God
wordNotes.explanation: Two compounds built on the same root for love frame a stark alternative. The comparison functions as “rather than,” excluding the second love. To be a lover of God is the heart of the first great commandment; to love pleasure in its place is idolatry in its everyday form.

The perfect participle pictures a mind wrapped in smoke, inflated and clouded by self-importance. Paul uses the verb of a novice elevated too soon and of a teacher who knows nothing yet dotes on disputes.

verses.bibleText: Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The final item in the catalogue is the most disturbing. The people Paul has described are not openly irreligious. They are “having a form of godliness.” In the Pastorals, godliness is the regular word for true Christian devotion (1 Timothy 3:16; 6:6), so Paul is describing people inside the church, or at least claiming its name. The vices of verses 2–4 can thrive beneath a respectable religious surface.

The word “form” denotes an outward shape or outline. Paul uses it in Romans of the person who has “the form of knowledge and of the truth in the law” while failing to live by it (Romans 2:20). Such religion keeps the visible features: attendance, vocabulary, perhaps even zeal for church activity. What it lacks is the inward reality that those features are meant to express.

“Denying the power thereof” uses a perfect participle, describing a settled refusal of the power that godliness carries. Power is a recurring theme of this letter. God has given his people a spirit “of power, and of love, and of a sound mind” (1:7), and Timothy is to suffer for the gospel “according to the power of God” (1:8). The gospel is itself “the power of God unto salvation” (Romans 1:16). The power of godliness is God’s grace at work, converting the heart, breaking sin’s hold, and producing a new life.

To deny it is to want the name of Christ without the new birth, and religion without repentance. Jesus spoke of people who honor him with their lips while their heart is far from him, and of others who call him Lord yet do not do the Father’s will (Matthew 7:21–23).

“From such turn away” is again present tense: keep turning away from them. This does not contradict the gentleness of 2:24–26. Timothy must still instruct opponents with meekness and pray for their repentance, but he must not grant such people influence, platform, or partnership in the work. He must also examine himself, since the warning applies to every heart that grows comfortable with religion while resisting its claims (2 Corinthians 13:5).

wordNotes.term: μόρφωσιν εὐσεβείας (morphōsin eusebeias) — a form of godliness
wordNotes.explanation: Morphōsis means an outward embodiment or outline. Paired with eusebeia, the Pastorals’ word for authentic devotion to God, it describes the visible shape of Christian religion without the reality that gives it life.

A present middle imperative found only here in the New Testament, it calls Timothy to keep turning himself away from such people. Similar counsel appears where Paul urges believers to mark and avoid those who cause division contrary to the doctrine they have learned.

verses.bibleText: For of this sort are they which creep into houses, and lead captive silly women laden with sins, led away with divers lusts,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For of this sort are they” narrows the focus from the general portrait to the false teachers at work in Ephesus. The shift to the present tense shows that Paul is no longer forecasting; he is describing what Timothy can already see.

These teachers “creep into houses.” The verb suggests slipping in unnoticed, worming one’s way inside. Since the church met in homes and was built around households, entrance into a home could give access to a whole congregation. Paul elsewhere speaks of teachers who “subvert whole houses” for gain (Titus 1:11), and Jude describes men who crept in unawares (Jude 1:4). “Lead captive” continues the military language of 2:26, where people are taken captive by the devil. The teachers act as his recruiting agents, taking prisoners.

“Silly women” renders a diminutive, literally “little women,” used here with contempt for a particular group, not for women as such. The same letter honors the faith of Lois and Eunice, through whom Timothy first knew the Scriptures (1:5; 3:15), and sends greetings to Prisca (4:19). What made these women vulnerable was their condition. They were “laden with sins,” a perfect participle picturing guilt heaped up until it overwhelms. A burdened conscience will grasp at any promised relief, especially one that offers spiritual novelty without the humbling path of confession and repentance. They were also “led away with divers lusts,” pulled in many directions by changing desires.

The verse exposes both the predator and the prey. Teachers who exploit the vulnerable betray the shepherd’s calling, and pastoral care must guard those whom guilt or loneliness has weakened. Yet the deeper remedy lies in the gospel itself. Unrelieved guilt makes people easy targets, but Christ invites the weary and heavy laden to come to him for rest (Matthew 11:28). A conscience cleansed by his forgiveness is far harder to capture.

wordNotes.explanation: A diminutive of the ordinary word for woman, it carries a disparaging tone, “weak” or “immature women.” The diminutive itself signals a specific group whose spiritual instability made them prey, not a judgment on women generally, as Paul’s praise of Timothy’s mother and grandmother shows.

wordNotes.term: σεσωρευμένα ἁμαρτίαις (sesōreumena hamartiais) — laden with sins
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to heap up, as coals are heaped on a head. The perfect tense describes a continuing condition of being weighed down, a conscience so burdened that it seizes whatever relief seems to be offered.

verses.bibleText: Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The people captured by these teachers become perpetual students who never graduate. They are “ever learning,” always hearing something new, yet “never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.” The two adverbs stand in deliberate opposition: always, never. “The knowledge of the truth” is a significant phrase in the Pastorals. God wills all men to be saved and to come to it (1 Timothy 2:4); repentance leads to it (2 Timothy 2:25); it accords with godliness (Titus 1:1). It means acknowledging and embracing the gospel so that it converts the life. Accumulated religious information is something else. One can gather opinions, speculations, and insights for years and still never submit to the truth that saves.

Two things explain the failure. The teaching itself is false, so the more it is absorbed the further the learner strays. And the learner is not seeking surrender. Jesus said that anyone willing to do God’s will shall know whether the teaching is from God (John 7:17). Understanding grows by obedience. When learning becomes a substitute for repentance, it hardens instead of healing. The Athenians who spent their time in nothing else but telling or hearing some new thing (Acts 17:21) illustrate the same restlessness. The warning reaches into every generation of the church. Bible study, sermons, and spiritual reading become another form of godliness without power if they never lead to a changed heart. The aim of learning is not novelty but Christ, known and obeyed.

wordNotes.term: ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας (epignōsin alētheias) — the knowledge of the truth
wordNotes.explanation: Epignōsis denotes full, acknowledged knowledge. In the Pastorals the phrase is linked with salvation, repentance, and godliness, so it describes the conversion that receives the gospel as true and lives by it.

verses.bibleText: Now as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these also resist the truth: men of corrupt minds, reprobate concerning the faith.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul illustrates the false teachers with an episode from Israel’s deliverance. When Moses and Aaron stood before Pharaoh, the court magicians reproduced the first signs “with their enchantments” (Exodus 7:11, 22). The Old Testament leaves them unnamed, but Jewish tradition remembered them as Jannes and Jambres, and the names were widely known in Paul’s day. Paul uses the familiar names to point to the biblical event, much as a preacher might name a well-known figure to make a point vivid.

The comparison lies in the method of opposition. The magicians did not deny that signs could happen; they imitated them. Their strategy was counterfeit, making the false look enough like the true that Pharaoh could dismiss God’s message. So the teachers in Ephesus, who keep a form of godliness, resist the truth by producing something that resembles it.

This has always been the deceiver’s way in the long conflict between Christ and Satan. Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light, and his ministers into ministers of righteousness (2 Corinthians 11:14–15). Scripture warns that before the end he will work signs and lying wonders (2 Thessalonians 2:9; Revelation 13:13–14).

To oppose Moses was to oppose the word God had given him. In the same way these teachers “resist the truth,” the gospel itself. Paul names the cause: they are “men of corrupt minds.” The perfect participle describes minds that have been ruined, and in the Pastorals the mind represents the whole moral and intellectual center of a person (1 Timothy 6:5; Titus 1:15). When that center is corrupted, judgment itself is bent.

They are also “reprobate concerning the faith.” The word means tested and found worthless, like metal that fails the assay. Timothy, by contrast, has been urged to show himself “approved unto God” (2:15). The two words come from the same root; one describes the teacher who passes God’s test, the other those who fail it.

wordNotes.term: Ἰάννης καὶ Ἰαμβρῆς (Iannēs kai Iambrēs) — Jannes and Jambres
wordNotes.explanation: These names, preserved in Jewish tradition, identify the leading magicians of Pharaoh’s court who copied the signs Moses performed. Paul’s point rests on the biblical account of their counterfeit opposition, not on legendary embellishment.

The word describes what has been tested and rejected as not genuine. It is the negative counterpart of dokimos, approved. Paul uses it of those whose profession fails the test and soberly applies the danger even to himself.

verses.bibleText: But they shall proceed no further: for their folly shall be manifest unto all men, as their's also was.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
After the warning comes reassurance. “They shall proceed no further” uses the same verb of progress found in 2:16, where error was said to advance into ungodliness. Here its reach is limited. The false teachers may capture some, but they will not overrun the church. The reason is that “their folly shall be manifest unto all men.” Folly means a lack of understanding, the mindlessness of teachers who do not grasp what they affirm (1 Timothy 1:7). The word for manifest is intensified: it will become plain, conspicuous, impossible to miss.

“As their’s also was” returns to Egypt. Pharaoh’s magicians kept pace with Moses for a time, but when Aaron struck the dust and it became lice, they failed and confessed, “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8:18–19). Later they could not even stand before Moses because of the boils (Exodus 9:11). Counterfeits have limits. They can imitate the outward appearance of God’s work, but they cannot reproduce its power. The timing belongs to God. Exposure may come gradually, through the barren fruit of a teaching, or fully only at the judgment, when the Lord will bring to light the hidden things of darkness (1 Corinthians 4:5). Timothy does not need to panic or adopt the methods of his opponents. Truth outlasts error.

wordNotes.explanation: Anoia is senselessness, a want of understanding; it describes the rage of opponents in the Gospels. Ekdēlos, found only here in the New Testament, strengthens the ordinary word for evident to mean thoroughly plain to everyone.

verses.bibleText: But thou hast fully known my doctrine, manner of life, purpose, faith, longsuffering, charity, patience,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But thou” turns sharply from the false teachers to Timothy. The pronoun is emphatic. Others resist the truth; Timothy has followed it, and he has followed it in the person of the apostle who taught him. “Hast fully known” translates a verb meaning to follow closely, to trace out, to make one’s own. Timothy has watched Paul long enough to know whether the man matched the message.

Nine items follow. “Doctrine” stands first, for Paul’s teaching is what most sharply contrasts with the errors just described. But teaching never stands alone, so he adds “manner of life,” his conduct in ordinary days, and “purpose,” the settled aim that directed his ministry. That aim he once summarized as finishing his course with joy and testifying the gospel of the grace of God (Acts 20:24). Then come “faith,” his dependence on God; “longsuffering,” patience with difficult people; “charity,” self-giving love; and “patience,” endurance under trial. Verse 11 will complete the list with his persecutions and afflictions.

This is not boasting. An aged prisoner near death sets out for his younger colleague the shape of a life that had been tested and found faithful. Paul had urged other churches to imitate him as he imitated Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1), and he could appeal to their own observation of how holily he had behaved among them (1 Thessalonians 2:10). The false teachers’ lives contradicted their claims; Paul’s life confirmed his. Every teacher of the gospel is weighed by that same measure.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to follow alongside and so to understand thoroughly, whether by personal presence or careful attention. It implies that Timothy has absorbed and embraced what he observed in Paul’s teaching and life.

Elsewhere this word usually describes God’s eternal purpose, as in the opening chapter of this letter. Applied to Paul, it denotes the resolved intention that governed his ministry, the steady aim of a heart set on cleaving to the Lord.

verses.bibleText: Persecutions, afflictions, which came unto me at Antioch, at Iconium, at Lystra; what persecutions I endured: but out of them all the Lord delivered me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul makes his endurance concrete by naming places. At Pisidian Antioch, opponents stirred up leading citizens and expelled Paul and Barnabas from the region (Acts 13:50). At Iconium, a plot to stone them forced them to flee (Acts 14:5–6). At Lystra, Paul was stoned and dragged out of the city, left for dead (Acts 14:19).

The choice of these early episodes is personal. Lystra was Timothy’s hometown, and he was well spoken of by the believers there and in Iconium (Acts 16:1–2). He had either witnessed these events or heard them recounted by those who had. When Paul returned through those cities, he strengthened the disciples by telling them that we must through much tribulation enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22). Timothy, then, had joined Paul knowing from the start what the gospel cost its messenger.

“What persecutions I endured” uses a verb meaning to bear up under a load. Paul does not claim to have escaped. “But out of them all the Lord delivered me” echoes the psalmist’s confidence that the Lord delivers the righteous out of all their afflictions (Psalm 34:19). The deliverance was out of the trials, not from ever entering them. God brought Paul through.

The same Lord who rescued him at Lystra would not keep him from the executioner in Rome. Yet Paul could still say, in his final chapter, that the Lord would deliver him from every evil work and preserve him unto his heavenly kingdom (4:18). The ultimate deliverance is resurrection to the kingdom at Christ’s appearing. God does not promise his servants freedom from suffering, but he never abandons them in it.

wordNotes.term: ἐκ πάντων με ἐρρύσατο ὁ κύριος (ek pantōn me errusato ho kyrios) — out of them all the Lord delivered me
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to rescue or snatch from danger, and the preposition ek indicates being brought out of trouble already entered. The wording closely recalls the Greek form of a psalm of deliverance.

Literally “I bore up under,” the verb pictures carrying a heavy weight without collapsing. Paul uses it of the strength God provides to bear temptation, and Peter of suffering wrongfully for conscience toward God.

verses.bibleText: Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
From his own experience Paul draws a general principle: “Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.” This is not a rule for apostles only or for an inner circle of especially devoted believers. “All” describes Christians as such, in distinction from those who keep only the form of godliness (v. 5). The form provokes no opposition; the reality does. “Will live” translates a verb of resolve. Those who determine to live godly, who set their wills toward faithfulness, meet resistance. Godliness exposes what darkness wants hidden. Jesus said that people love darkness because their deeds are evil and hate the light that reveals them (John 3:19–20), and he told his disciples that if the world hated him it would hate them also (John 15:18–20). Behind human hostility stands the dragon who makes war with those who keep the commandments of God and have the testimony of Jesus (Revelation 12:17).

The phrase “in Christ Jesus” is essential. A godly life does not grow from human effort; it is life lived in union with Christ, drawing its strength and pattern from him. He is also the first to suffer. To share his life is to share in some measure his rejection, and Scripture treats this as a privilege given to believers (Philippians 1:29).

Persecution takes many forms: ridicule, exclusion, economic loss, legal penalty, or violence. Not every hardship qualifies. Peter warns that suffering as an evildoer brings no credit, while suffering as a Christian glorifies God (1 Peter 4:15–16). Believers should never invite opposition by harshness. Yet when faithfulness brings it, they should not be surprised, as though something strange had happened (1 Peter 4:12).

wordNotes.term: θέλοντες εὐσεβῶς ζῆν (thelontes eusebōs zēn) — that will live godly
wordNotes.explanation: The participle expresses settled desire and purpose, and the adverb describes a life of reverent devotion to God. Paul elsewhere teaches that the grace of God trains believers to live godly in this present world.
The future passive states a certainty: they will be persecuted. The same expectation runs from the teaching of Jesus through Paul’s first missionary journey to his earliest letters.

verses.bibleText: But evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Over against those who live godly, Paul sets “evil men and seducers.” The second word originally meant sorcerers or wizards and came to describe impostors and swindlers. It may echo the Egyptian magicians of verse 8, and it would have carried weight in Ephesus, where books of magic had once been burned in public (Acts 19:19). The term describes those who draw people into impiety while using pious words.

Such people “shall wax worse and worse,” literally “make progress toward the worse.” The irony is sharp. Like the teachers of 2:16, they advance, but only downward. Verse 9 said their influence would not spread without limit; this verse says their character will deteriorate. Evil grows more intense even where it does not grow more extensive. Habits of sin, repeated, become harder to break, and only the grace of God can reverse that course (Jeremiah 13:23).

“Deceiving, and being deceived” describes the trap. Those who lead others astray are themselves led astray. They come to believe their own falsehoods, and behind them stands the one who deceives the whole world (Revelation 12:9). Paul elsewhere warns that those who refuse the love of the truth become susceptible to strong delusion (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11). The verse removes any illusion that history will drift steadily toward goodness. The conflict sharpens toward the end. That is why the next words are so urgent: “But continue thou.”

wordNotes.explanation: Originally a term for sorcerers who muttered incantations, it came to mean impostors who deceive by trickery. Found only here in the New Testament, it fits a passage that has compared false teachers with the magicians of Egypt.

wordNotes.term: πλανῶντες καὶ πλανώμενοι (planōntes kai planōmenoi) — deceiving, and being deceived
wordNotes.explanation: The same verb appears first active and then passive: they cause others to wander and are themselves made to wander. The deceiver of the world reproduces his work through those who yield to him.

verses.bibleText: But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But continue thou” sets Timothy against the downward progress of verse 13. Evil men advance toward the worse; Timothy is to remain. The verb means to stay, abide, keep one’s place. Faithfulness here is not restless movement toward the next new idea but steady perseverance in what is true.

This is no appeal to mere habit or tradition. Timothy has “learned” these things and “hast been assured of” them. The second verb means to be convinced, to have become persuaded that something is trustworthy. His faith was tested, examined, and embraced. Paul asks him to hold to convictions he already knows to be well founded, unlike the perpetual learners of verse 7 who never arrive.

“Knowing of whom thou hast learned them” grounds that assurance in the character of his teachers. The best manuscripts read a plural, “from whom,” pointing to Paul, whose life Timothy had followed (v. 10), and to Lois and Eunice, who taught him in childhood (1:5). The integrity of a teacher commends the teaching; Timothy had seen the truth lived out by those who passed it on. Yet even these teachers point beyond themselves. Verse 15 immediately names the Scriptures as the source of what they taught. Personal trust in godly teachers is valuable, but faith must finally rest on the word of God, which stands even if a respected messenger should fail (Galatians 1:8). Jesus said that those who continue in his word are his disciples indeed (John 8:31).

wordNotes.explanation: The present imperative of the verb “to remain” calls for ongoing steadfastness. In John’s writings the same verb describes abiding in Christ and letting the message heard from the beginning abide in the believer.

Found only here in the New Testament, the verb means to be made confident or convinced of something as trustworthy. It describes conviction formed by instruction and experience, the settled faith of one rooted and established.

verses.bibleText: And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Timothy’s acquaintance with Scripture reached back “from a child,” literally from infancy. His mother and grandmother were Jewish believers, and they did what faithful Israelite homes had long been commanded to do: they taught God’s words diligently to their children, speaking of them in the house and by the way (Deuteronomy 6:6–7). Though his father was Greek (Acts 16:1), Timothy grew up with Israel’s Scriptures as the furniture of his mind.

“The holy scriptures” translates a phrase that Greek-speaking Jews used for their sacred writings, the books we call the Old Testament. They are holy because they come from God and are set apart from every other writing. When Paul wrote, the New Testament had not yet been gathered, though gospel accounts and apostolic letters were circulating.

These Scriptures “are able to make thee wise unto salvation.” The participle describes an inherent capacity, and it stands in pointed contrast with the women of verse 7, who were “never able” to come to the truth.

Scripture’s central purpose is to lead people to salvation. It records history, gives law, and reveals God’s character, but all of this serves the aim of bringing sinners to the Saviour. Jesus opened the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms to show what was written concerning himself (Luke 24:27, 44), and he told his hearers that the Scriptures testify of him (John 5:39).

The saving wisdom is received “through faith which is in Christ Jesus.” Scripture instructs; faith receives. Knowledge of the text, however extensive, does not save by itself. The very scholars who searched the Scriptures most carefully could refuse to come to Christ for life (John 5:40). The Old Testament was therefore no outdated preparation for Timothy. It was a gospel book, pointing to the one in whom it is fulfilled, and it continues to serve the church in that way, written for our learning that we might have hope (Romans 15:4).

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “sacred writings,” this was a familiar designation among Greek-speaking Jews for the Hebrew Scriptures. It emphasizes their sacred origin and character, the oracles of God entrusted to Israel and promised beforehand through the prophets.

wordNotes.term: σοφίσαι εἰς σωτηρίαν (sophisai eis sōtērian) — to make wise unto salvation
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to instruct or make wise, and the preposition points toward a goal. Scripture gives the understanding that leads a person to salvation, as the psalmist said the testimony of the Lord makes wise the simple.

verses.bibleText: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now states the ground of Scripture’s saving power. “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” renders a single Greek word, theopneustos, meaning “God-breathed.” Scripture is the product of God’s breath, as surely as the heavens were made by the breath of his mouth (Psalm 33:6) and the first man became a living soul when God breathed into him (Genesis 2:7). The Bible does not merely contain thoughts about God; it is breathed out by God.

Two questions of wording deserve attention. “All scripture” may also be rendered “every scripture,” but the difference is slight: the whole and each of its parts are in view. Some have proposed reading “every inspired scripture is also profitable,” as though some writings within Scripture might lack inspiration. That reading is grammatically possible but unlikely. The same construction in 1 Timothy 4:4 places both adjectives in the predicate, and “scripture” in the New Testament always refers to the sacred writings. The natural sense is that all Scripture is God-breathed and profitable. No reader is authorized to sift the Bible, accepting what he judges inspired and setting aside the rest.

Inspiration did not erase the human writers. Peter explains that holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Ghost (2 Peter 1:21). God worked through their language, experience, and personality, yet what they wrote is his word. Paul’s primary reference is to the Old Testament, but the principle reaches further. Paul quotes a saying of Jesus alongside Deuteronomy as “scripture” (1 Timothy 5:18), and Peter counts Paul’s letters among the Scriptures (2 Peter 3:15–16).

Because it is God-breathed, Scripture is “profitable” in four ways. “Doctrine” is positive teaching of what is true. “Reproof” exposes error and convicts of sin. “Correction” restores what has gone wrong, setting a life upright again. “Instruction in righteousness” is training, the word used for a father’s nurture of his children (Ephesians 6:4), forming right conduct over time. The first pair concerns belief, the second behavior, and each pair moves between building up and tearing down. The same four tasks reappear in the charge to preach the word, reprove, rebuke, and exhort (4:2).

Here is the church’s standard. Teaching, tradition, experience, and every claim to spiritual insight must be measured by the word God has breathed out: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isaiah 8:20).

wordNotes.term: θεόπνευστος (theopneustos) — given by inspiration of God
wordNotes.explanation: This compound of “God” and “breathe” appears nowhere else in the Bible. Verbal adjectives of this kind compounded with “God” normally describe what God produces, so the word presents Scripture as breathed out by God, not merely as writing that breathes religious sentiment. It affirms both the divine origin and the authority of the whole.

Epanorthōsis, found only here in the New Testament, means setting upright again, restoring to a right state. Paideia is the discipline and training of a child, the formation that yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness in those exercised by it.

verses.bibleText: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The word “That” introduces the purpose for which God made Scripture profitable. Its fourfold work aims at a person: “the man of God.” In the Old Testament this title belonged to prophets and leaders such as Moses and Elijah (Deuteronomy 33:1; 1 Kings 17:24), people who belonged to God and spoke for him. Paul has already applied it to Timothy (1 Timothy 6:11), and it fits with special force a minister of the word. Yet it describes every believer who belongs wholly to God.

“Perfect” translates artios, meaning fit, capable, able to meet every demand. It does not describe sinless perfection but complete readiness. “Throughly furnished” comes from the same root with an intensifying prefix, meaning fully equipped or outfitted. The perfect participle presents this as a settled state that Scripture produces.

The goal is “all good works.” Scripture’s teaching ends in action. Earlier Paul spoke of a vessel “prepared unto every good work” (2:21), and believers are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10). The word that makes wise unto salvation also trains the saved for service.

The verse affirms the sufficiency of Scripture. Everything necessary for salvation and godly living is supplied in the God-breathed word, and it stands as the final standard of faith and practice. This does not set aside the Spirit, who inspired the Scriptures, opens them to the reader (John 16:13), and still gives gifts to the church, prophecy among them (1 Thessalonians 5:20-21). It does mean that every later message claiming his name must agree with what he has written and be tested by it (Isaiah 8:20). From here Paul moves directly to the charge, “Preach the word” (4:2).

wordNotes.term: ἄρτιος … ἐξηρτισμένος (artios … exērtismenos) — perfect, throughly furnished
wordNotes.explanation: Artios describes one fitted and capable for a task. The participle, built on the same root, intensifies the idea: completely equipped and ready. The pairing stresses that Scripture leaves the servant of God lacking nothing needed for his work.

wordNotes.term: ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος (ho tou theou anthrōpos) — the man of God
wordNotes.explanation: An Old Testament title for those who belonged to God and spoke his word, applied in the New Testament only to Timothy. It marks a life defined by allegiance to God and fitted for his service.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: How can a person be thoroughly religious and still be untouched by the power of God?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: In an age when self-love wears the clothing of godliness and deception grows worse, believers stand firm by abiding in the God-breathed Scriptures that lead to salvation in Christ and equip for every good work.
discussionQuestions: Why does Paul begin and end his list of vices with words about love, and what does that reveal about the root of sin?
What marks the difference between a form of godliness and its power in practical life?
How does the example of Pharaoh’s magicians help believers recognize counterfeit spirituality?
Why does Paul treat persecution as normal for those who live godly in Christ Jesus?
What does it mean in daily practice for Scripture to teach, reprove, correct, and train?
commonMisunderstandings: The last days are not a distant period unrelated to the apostles; they began with Christ’s first coming and intensify toward his return.
The phrase “silly women” describes particular people made vulnerable by guilt and desire, not women in general, whom this same letter honors in Lois and Eunice.
Being “perfect” in verse 17 means fully equipped for God’s service, not sinless or beyond growth.
Inspiration does not belong only to selected passages that readers judge worthy; all Scripture is God-breathed.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the warning and the remedy together: Paul’s realistic picture of the age is answered by a faithful life and an inspired Scripture sufficient to make believers wise unto salvation and ready for every good work.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Turn from religion that keeps the name and refuses the power, and give the God-breathed word daily room to teach, reprove, correct, and train you in Christ.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: The Scriptures, breathed out by God, reveal the way of salvation through faith in Christ Jesus and supply the power that empty religion lacks.
flow: Human beings left to themselves turn their love inward toward self, money, and pleasure.
Even religion can become an outward shell that resists God’s transforming power.
God has spoken in Scripture, which he himself breathed out, to make people wise unto salvation.
That salvation is received through faith in Christ Jesus, not through religious knowledge alone.
The same word then trains the believer in righteousness and prepares him for every good work.
simpleIllustrations: A lamp can be beautifully shaped and properly placed, yet without connection to power it gives no light.
Pharaoh’s magicians could imitate some signs, but when God’s work went beyond their tricks the difference became plain to everyone.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you let the God-breathed Scriptures lead you to Christ and receive from him the power that a merely outward religion can never supply?
cautions: Do not use the vice list to condemn others while ignoring how self-love works in your own heart.
Do not imply that knowing Bible facts saves apart from faith in Christ Jesus.
Do not present persecution as proof of faithfulness when suffering results from harshness or wrongdoing.

reflectionQuestions: Which of my loves—self, money, pleasure, or God—actually governs my choices this week?
Where might I be keeping the form of godliness while resisting its power to change me?
Am I ever learning without coming to obey what I learn?
What cost am I willing to bear for living godly in Christ Jesus?
How am I letting Scripture correct and train me, not merely inform me?
